effective-hourly-rate.html.text:
Quote Margin Check

How to calculate your effective hourly rate on a fixed-price quote

A fixed-price quote can look good until the hours you do not invoice separately are included. Your effective hourly rate is the amount left for your work divided by every hour the project is expected to consume.

1. Count every project hour

Add delivery work, administration, and revisions. Administration includes calls, project management, proposals, invoicing, and handoff. If you expect to spend time on it, include it in the estimate.

total hours = delivery hours + admin hours + revision hours

2. Count direct costs

List costs that belong to this project, such as subcontractor work, project-specific tools, and materials. Keep the currency and assumptions consistent with the quote.

direct costs = overhead + subcontractor cost

3. Calculate the effective hourly rate

Subtract direct costs from the quoted price, then divide by total hours. This is an arithmetic view of the supplied assumptions, not a promise that the project will be profitable.

effective hourly rate = (quoted price - direct costs) / total hours

4. Compare with your target rate

To estimate the price needed for your supplied target rate, multiply total hours by that rate and add direct costs.

target price = (total hours × target hourly rate) + direct costs

On the calculator example — $2,400 quoted, 35 hours, $480 of direct costs, $75 target — the leftover rate is $54.86/hour and the price that would hold $75/hour is $3,105. That is arithmetic on the supplied figures, not advice to raise the quote.

Use the free Quote Margin Check calculator to change the assumptions and review overrun scenarios before sending the quote. Your own scope, cost, and rate decisions remain yours.

if-costs-go-up-is-this-quote-still-alive.text:
← Quote Margin Check

If costs go up, is this quote still alive?

Freelancers search this after a supplier or a sub comes back higher than the figure they baked into a fixed price. Time-overrun tables answer a different question — extra hours. This page holds hours still and moves only overhead plus subcontractor cost.

Open the Quote Margin Check calculator and keep your own price, hours, and target rate. The table below uses the page defaults: $2,400 quoted, 24 delivery + 5 admin + 6 revision hours, $180 overhead, $300 subcontractor, $75/hour target.

The example quote, then a cost rise

As quoted, $480 of direct costs leaves $54.86/hour and a $705 gap below the $3,105 target price. A 25% rise in those costs is $120 more cash out — not 25% of the $2,400 quote. The effective rate falls to $51.43/hour. Holding $75/hour would take $3,225.

Cost rise Direct costs Effective rate Price to hold $75/hour Gap to target
As quoted$480.00$54.86/hour$3,105.00−$705.00
+10%$528.00$53.49/hour$3,153.00−$753.00
+25%$600.00$51.43/hour$3,225.00−$825.00
+50%$720.00$48.00/hour$3,345.00−$945.00

When there is nothing left

A $1,000 quote with $800 of overhead and a $80 target already leaves $20/hour. At +50% the same overhead is $1,200, so the quote no longer covers direct costs (−$20/hour). The table will show a negative rate rather than hiding it.

Enter the numbers from your own estimate. This page does not forecast supplier prices, recommend a markup, or claim a quote is profitable.

Common questions

What happens to a fixed-price quote if materials go up after I send it?

The customer price stays the same. Extra overhead and subcontractor cost come out of the amount left for your hours. On the calculator example ($2,400, 35 hours, $480 of direct costs, $75 target), a 25% cost rise drops the effective rate from $54.86 to $51.43/hour. Holding $75/hour would take a $3,225 quote instead of $2,400.

Is a 10% cost rise a 10% hit to my hourly rate?

No. The rise applies only to overhead and subcontractor cost, not to the whole quote. On the example, +10% is $48 more of direct cost, so the effective rate falls from $54.86 to $53.49 — not 10%.

Does this predict supplier prices?

No. The table is arithmetic on the figures you typed. Enter your own overhead and subcontractor numbers. It is not tax, financial, or pricing advice.

if-they-ask-for-10-percent-off.html.text:
← Quote Margin Check

If they ask for 10% off, what rate is left?

Freelancers search this after a “can you do 10%?” email on a quote they already sent. Time-overrun tables answer extra hours. Cost-rise tables answer a more expensive sub. This page holds hours and costs still and moves only the quoted price.

Open the Quote Margin Check calculator and keep your own price, hours, and target rate. The table below uses the page defaults: $2,400 quoted, 24 delivery + 5 admin + 6 revision hours, $180 overhead, $300 subcontractor, $75/hour target.

The example quote, then a 10% ask

As quoted, $480 of direct costs leaves $54.86/hour and a $705 gap below the $3,105 target price. Ten percent off is $240 less cash in — not 10% of the leftover. The effective rate falls to $48.00/hour. Holding $75/hour would take cutting 12.60 hours of scope (22.40 hours of work left). Even at the full $2,400 the same target already wants 9.40 hours cut; the discount adds 3.20 more.

Discount Price Effective rate Hours to cut to hold $75/hour Gap to target
As quoted$2,400.00$54.86/hour9.40 hours−$705.00
5% off$2,280.00$51.43/hour11.00 hours−$825.00
10% off$2,160.00$48.00/hour12.60 hours−$945.00
15% off$2,040.00$44.57/hour14.20 hours−$1,065.00
20% off$1,920.00$41.14/hour15.80 hours−$1,185.00

When the discount no longer covers costs

A $1,000 quote with $800 of overhead and an $80 target already leaves $20/hour. At 50% off the price is $500, so the quote no longer covers direct costs (−$30/hour). Cutting hours cannot fix that — there is nothing left for your time. The table will say so rather than hiding it.

Enter the numbers from your own estimate. This page does not recommend accepting or refusing a discount, write a reply, or claim a quote is profitable.

Common questions

What happens to my effective hourly rate if a client asks for 10% off?

Hours and direct costs stay the same. Only the quoted price falls. On the calculator example ($2,400, 35 hours, $480 of direct costs, $75 target), 10% off is $2,160 and $48.00/hour. Holding $75/hour would take cutting 12.60 hours of scope (22.40 hours of work left).

Is 10% off a 10% hit to my hourly rate?

No. The discount applies to the whole price, but your overhead and subcontractor cost do not shrink with it. On the example the rate falls from $54.86 to $48.00 — more than 10% — because the $480 of direct costs is unchanged.

Does this tell me whether to accept the discount?

No. The table is arithmetic on the figures you typed. It does not recommend a price, write a negotiation script, or claim a quote is profitable. You decide what rate and scope are acceptable.

      What this checks

      Fixed-price quotes usually price the visible delivery work and quietly skip the rest: admin time, revision rounds, overhead, and subcontractor costs. This calculator adds all of it back in and reports the effective hourly rate you're actually being paid — alongside the price you'd need to charge to hit your own target rate.

      It does not recommend a price, does not provide tax or financial advice, and does not claim a quote is profitable. The gap to target price, after direct costs, and fixed vs hourly figures are arithmetic comparisons only — you decide what costs, target rate, and billing model are appropriate for the job.

      The fixed-vs-hourly table answers the pre-send fork that the overrun rows alone cannot: if this work slips, does the extra time come out of your rate, or does the client pay it? Planned hours are included so you can see whether the fixed quote is already a discount versus hourly at your target, before any overrun.

      It also shows what happens if overhead and subcontractor costs rise +10%, +25%, or +50% before you start. Hours and the quoted price stay fixed — the table is the cash you lose, or the new price that would still hit your target rate. That is not a forecast of supplier prices. See if costs go up, is this quote still alive.

      A third table keeps hours and costs fixed and knocks 5–20% off the quoted price. That is the “can you do 10%?” email. It shows the new effective rate and how many hours of scope would have to leave to still hit your target rate. It is not a negotiation script. See if they ask for 10% off.

      A fourth table puts the same hours and direct costs next to hourly at your target rate. Planned hours answers whether the fixed quote is already a discount versus hourly; extra-time rows show how the two bills diverge when the work runs long. It is not a recommendation of which to send. See should I send a fixed quote or bill hourly.

      A fifth table is the mid-project cancel. Type hours already spent, cash already collected, a kill fee on top of that, and costs that are already sunk. It shows cash kept if you finish, cash kept if you take the fee, and cash kept if you walk with only the deposit — then the same three paths if the freed hours could be rebooked at your target rate. It does not tell you to cancel or finish. See should I take this kill fee or finish.

      New to the arithmetic? The short guide how to calculate your effective hourly rate walks the hours, direct costs, leftover rate, and target price. See also this calculator vs. Bonsai, or this calculator vs. tracking quotes in a spreadsheet.

      Copy or download a plain-text review summary for an email or proposal note, or copy or download the current review as a spreadsheet-safe CSV. Currency labels with commas or quotes stay in one cell, and the file includes the time-overrun, cost-rise, discount-ask, fixed-vs-hourly, and kill-fee rows shown above. Prefer the command line, or need to batch several quotes? The same logic ships as a Python CLI (in this repository) that reads/writes JSON, Markdown, and CSV.

      Common questions

      How do I calculate my effective hourly rate on a fixed-price quote?

      Add up every hour the project will actually take you — delivery work, admin, and revisions — then subtract any direct costs (overhead, subcontractors) from the price, and divide what's left by the total hours. That is your effective hourly rate: what you're really being paid per hour once every task is counted, not just the billable delivery hours.

      Why does a quote that looks profitable still underpay me?

      Fixed-price quotes usually price only the visible delivery work. Admin time (calls, invoicing, project management), revision rounds, and subcontractor or tool costs quietly eat into the same fixed price, so the effective hourly rate ends up well below the rate you meant to charge.

      What if materials or a subcontractor quote go up after I send a fixed price?

      Keep the quoted price and hours fixed and raise only overhead plus subcontractor cost. The calculator shows the new effective hourly rate and the price that would still hit your target rate at +10%, +25%, and +50%. That is arithmetic on your inputs, not a forecast of supplier prices.

      What if the client asks for 10% off a fixed-price quote?

      Keep hours and direct costs fixed and lower only the quoted price. On the calculator example ($2,400, 35 hours, $480 of direct costs, $75 target), 10% off is $2,160 and $48.00/hour. Holding $75/hour would take cutting 12.60 hours of scope. That is arithmetic on your inputs, not a negotiation script.

      Should I send a fixed-price quote or bill hourly?

      Compare the same hours and direct costs both ways. A fixed quote stays the same if the work runs long; hourly bills those hours at your target rate plus the same costs. On the calculator example ($2,400, 35 hours, $480 of direct costs, $75 target), hourly at planned hours would bill $3,105 — $705 more than the fixed quote. That is arithmetic on your inputs, not a recommendation of which to send.

      Should I take a kill fee or finish the remaining hours?

      Compare cash kept if you finish, cash kept if you take the kill fee, and cash kept if you walk with only what is already paid. On the calculator example ($2,400, 35 hours, $480 of costs, 14 hours already spent, $1,200 already paid, $360 kill fee, $180 sunk), finishing keeps $1,920.00 — $540.00 more cash than the kill fee. Booking the 21 freed hours at $75/hour would make the kill fee $1,035.00 ahead. That is arithmetic on your inputs, not advice to cancel or finish.

Should I send a fixed quote or bill hourly?

Freelancers search this after a client asks “can you just give me a number?” Time-overrun tables show what extra hours do to a fixed rate. This page puts the same hours next to hourly at your target so you can see both bills before you send either one.

Open the Quote Margin Check calculator and keep your own price, hours, and target rate. The table below uses the page defaults: $2,400 quoted, 24 delivery + 5 admin + 6 revision hours, $180 overhead, $300 subcontractor, $75/hour target.

The example quote, then hourly at the same hours

As quoted, $480 of direct costs leaves $54.86/hour and a $705 gap below the $3,105 target price. Hourly at that same target would bill $3,105 — $705 more than the fixed quote. That is not “should send hourly.” It is the cash difference if the client paid the supplied target rate for the same hours.

Extra time Hours Fixed effective rate Hourly bill Hourly minus fixed
planned35.00$54.86/hour$3,105.00$705.00
+10%38.50$49.87/hour$3,367.50$967.50
+25%43.75$43.89/hour$3,761.25$1,361.25
+50%52.50$36.57/hour$4,417.50$2,017.50

When the fixed quote is already above hourly

A $2,000 quote for 10 hours at a $100 target with no direct costs already bills $1,000 more than hourly ($2,000 vs $1,000). Extra hours still grow the hourly bill while the fixed price stays put. The table will show a negative “hourly minus fixed” rather than hiding that the fixed quote is the higher bill.

Enter the numbers from your own estimate. This page does not recommend a billing model, write a proposal, or claim a quote is profitable.

Common questions

Should I send a fixed-price quote or bill hourly?

Compare the same hours and direct costs both ways. A fixed quote stays the same if the work runs long; hourly bills those hours at your target rate plus the same costs. On the calculator example ($2,400, 35 hours, $480 of direct costs, $75 target), hourly at planned hours would bill $3,105 — $705 more than the fixed quote.

Does extra time change the comparison?

Yes for hourly, no for the fixed price. At +50% hours (52.50 hours) the fixed effective rate falls to $36.57/hour while hourly would bill $4,417.50 — $2,017.50 more than the $2,400 quote. The extra hours are eaten on the fixed path and billed on the hourly path.

Does this tell me which billing model to send?

No. The table is arithmetic on the figures you typed. It does not recommend a billing model, write a proposal, or claim a quote is profitable. You decide what to send.

should-i-take-this-kill-fee-or-finish.ht.text:
← Quote Margin Check

Should I take this kill fee or finish the remaining hours?

Freelancers search this after a client pauses the project, “goes in another direction,” or asks to stop at 40% done. Discount tables answer a cheaper quote. Cost-rise tables answer a more expensive sub. This page holds the original price still and moves only how much work is left, how much cash is already in, and what they offered to walk away.

Open the Quote Margin Check calculator and keep your own price, hours, deposit, kill fee, and sunk costs. The table below uses the page defaults: $2,400 quoted, 24 delivery + 5 admin + 6 revision hours, $180 overhead, $300 subcontractor, $75/hour target, 14 hours already spent, $1,200 already paid, $360 kill fee, $180 already sunk.

Finish keeps more cash. The fee wins only if you refill the hours.

As quoted, $480 of direct costs leaves $1,920.00 if they pay the rest. Fourteen hours are already spent and $180 of overhead is already gone. Finishing the remaining 21.00 hours still collects $1,200.00 and still spends the $300 sub — $900.00 from here, $42.86/hour.

The $360 kill fee on top of the $1,200 deposit keeps $1,380.00 after sunk costs — $540.00 less cash than finishing. Walking with only the deposit keeps $1,020.00. If those 21 hours can be rebooked at $75/hour ($1,575.00), the kill fee is $1,035.00 ahead of finishing. If they stay empty, finish.

Path Cash kept Vs finishing Hours freed If you refill at $75/hour
Finish remaining work$1,920.00—0.00$1,920.00
Take the kill fee$1,380.00−$540.0021.00$2,955.00
Walk with only what's paid$1,020.00−$900.0021.00$2,595.00

When the remaining invoice no longer covers remaining costs

Same quote, but they already paid $2,160 and you have only spent 8 hours. An $80 kill fee on top of that keeps $2,060.00. Finishing the last 27 hours collects $240 more and still spends $300 of remaining costs — −$60.00 from here. The kill fee already keeps $140.00 more cash than finishing, before any refill.

Enter the hours, deposit, fee, and sunk costs from your own job. This page does not recommend taking or refusing a kill fee, write a cancellation clause, or claim other work will appear.

Common questions

Should I take a kill fee or finish a cancelled freelance project?

On a typical $2,400 quote (35 hours, $480 of costs) with 14 hours already spent, $1,200 already paid, $180 of costs already sunk, and a $360 kill fee, finishing keeps $1,920.00. The kill fee keeps $1,380.00 — $540.00 less cash. Walking with only the deposit keeps $1,020.00. Finishing the remaining 21.00 hours pays $900.00 from here ($42.86/hour). Booking those 21 hours at $75/hour would make the kill fee $1,035.00 ahead of finishing.

When does a kill fee already keep more cash than finishing?

When most of the price is already paid and remaining costs are still open. On the same $2,400 quote with 8 hours spent, $2,160 already paid, $180 sunk, and an $80 kill fee, finishing the last 27 hours collects only $240 more and still spends $300 of remaining costs — $60 from here. The kill fee keeps $2,060.00, $140.00 more cash than finishing.

vs-bonsai.html.text:
← Quote Margin Check

This calculator vs. Bonsai

Two different shapes: Bonsai runs your whole freelance business — proposals, contracts, time tracking, invoicing — as an ongoing subscription account. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what does this quote actually pay per hour, once every task is counted — before you send it.

What each tool is for

Bonsai is client-management software, sold under an ongoing subscription account to freelancers and small agencies running a full client roster. It builds and sends proposals and contracts with e-signatures, tracks billable and non-billable time across every project, generates and chases invoices, tracks expenses, and estimates quarterly taxes in supported regions, all synced across every client you run. Setting it up means creating an account and configuring your proposal, contract, and invoice templates — not a one-off calculation. Bonsai's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, feature tiers, or pricing, so only its well-documented category and identity are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not send proposals, collect e-signatures, track time across a roster, or chase invoices. It takes one proposed quote — price, delivery hours, admin and revision time, overhead, and subcontractor cost — and works out the effective hourly rate you are really being paid once every hidden task is counted, the price that hits your target rate, what a requested discount or a scope change actually costs, and what a mid-project cancellation is worth compared with finishing. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and nothing you type is uploaded.

vs-tracking-quotes-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Quote Margin Check

This calculator vs. tracking quotes in a spreadsheet

Effective hourly rate, a cost rise, a discount ask, fixed-vs-hourly, a kill fee, and a price ladder are each ordinary arithmetic. This page names no specific product — it compares against the generic method of building that arithmetic in a spreadsheet, and says where a spreadsheet still wins.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs: total hours to an effective rate, a target price at a chosen hourly rate, what a cost rise or a client's discount ask does to that rate, fixed pay minus what the same hours would earn billed hourly, what finishing beats a kill fee by, and a price ladder across a range of target rates. Building it means one formula per scenario, in its own section, and a new section the next time the quote needs a decision the sheet does not already have.

This calculator keeps all six of those scenarios wired to the same quote, so typing one number — the price, the hours, a requested discount — recomputes every panel at once instead of six formulas one at a time. A shareable link carries the whole quote in the URL itself, so sending someone the scenario is a link instead of a file two people have to keep in sync. And when you do want the numbers in a sheet, the page exports a spreadsheet-safe CSV, a Markdown review, or a JSON report in one click, so building the sheet is optional rather than the only way in.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. Effective hourly rate, a cost rise, a discount ask, fixed-vs-hourly billing, a kill fee, and a target-rate price ladder are all ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Building it means one formula per scenario, and rebuilding a section the next time the quote needs a decision the sheet does not already have — a client asking for 10% off, a mid-project cancellation, a cost that rose before the work started.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Keep all six scenarios wired to the same quote so a discount ask, a kill fee, and a cost rise recompute from one edit instead of six separate formula updates. It also produces a shareable link that carries the whole quote in the URL itself, and CSV, Markdown, and JSON exports for the moment you do want the numbers in a sheet, without building the sheet first.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, for tracking many quotes over time in one place, or for a fee structure this tool's inputs cannot represent — a retainer with a rolling discount, a multi-currency contract, revenue share instead of a flat price. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one quote's effective rate, right now.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your figures in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, and the optional local history and usage counters stay on this device.
